[Question] Why does Shovel Knight take up few hundred Mbs of storage space? Could the amount of space taken be reduced to at least 50fold?
Because the game engine is more complex that it let on, I'd guess...

Shovel Knight does an amazing job at looking and acting like an old game, but it is in fact a modern game in disguise. It has much higher sound quality, a more advanced engine, and much richer colour variety than older games. Old games also tend to reuse assets a lot more often than Shovel Knight does, and do not have as many tile set variants.

I think a lot of people tend to underestimate the degree of cleverness that had to be applied in order to make older games happen. There's a reason there are so many more gamers out there now than there used to be back then--building a videogame out of base principles on modest hardware is very different than grabbing RPG maker (or even OpenGL) and putting things out there.

Now, don't get me wrong--I think the fact that creators "have it easy" these days is an awesome thing, and the explosion of amazing content we've seen is proof of that. People who are really great at writing mathematical poetry in software are few, far between, and they tend not to tell great stories.

But, if you're into that kind of thing, looking at the stuff they did was inspiring.

The fact that games like Pokemon Red/Blue and Gold/Silver were able to fit into such small memory space back in the day truly was a marvel.

You are totally correct that if it was still that difficult there would be fewer games, fewer of them would be quality, and they'd all be expensive.

If you read the story about the trouble creating Gold and Silver and how Nintendo sent Iwata in as their secret programming weapon to help with storing all that data on one tiny cartridge, it makes you miss the man even more.
True. People often remember him for the quirky TV spots he did, but Iwata was a coding genius. It's a shame that it's always the good ones that go early.

Yep. It's not just the assets, but the overall system requirements are much higher. Back in the day, lots of time was spent on optimization. Lots of programming tricks were required just to get sufficient performance, and common things like health and ammo were each squeezed into a single byte (0-255) because of limit memory. These days, we have fast video cards, multi-core processors and cheap RAM and hard drives. Any PC or console these days would be overkill for a game like Shovel Knight, so the devs just let loose and focus on making a really good game.

Shovel Knight also fixes certain bugs and glitches with were common in old platformers due to hardware limitations. In a lot of games only 1 entity could exist on each horizontal plane, which meant that to hold 2 on the same plane developers had to quickly flicker each entity so both were visible, but both were visibly flickering. Shovel Knight has eliminated this issue.
The amount and quality of the music probably heavily contributes to the file size.

Devs during the 8-bit era had to pull some serious shenanigans to get their games to work. Back in the 80s, the ability to make video games was an extremely rare talent, because of all the bullshit necessary to make the graphics (particularly colors) and sound work correctly.

The same thing that opened up gaming opened up computer-advancement in general; excess resources. Long time ago, one-hot encoding (a way of designing circuits that made them less complex and much easier to understand) was considered useless; it used too many expensive components for what it accomplished. Nowadays? It's pretty tricky to find a circuit that isn't designed using one-hot.

There's no reason to optimize your game to take up less space when it's already considered miniscule by modern standards.
